note: The guitar-advanced week: a mode is drilled by the one note that sets it apart, and that method is the key skill on all seven days in new forms (Dorian's 6th against natural minor, as the 3rd of D7, in three joined positions, Mixolydian's ♭7 by the same method, the two modes one note apart in the same frets, Dorian moved to D, then the jam). Triads on every string set, 9th chords and comping over drums and bass feed the solos, warm-ups climb in choice stages, and each why is a fact the student can build the next drill from.

plan.title: Week 1: one note makes the mode
plan.summary: Find the one note that sets a mode apart, then aim for it: the 6th in Dorian, the ♭7 in Mixolydian, in A and then in D. Triads on every string set and 9th chords give your solos places to land, and each day ends over a band.
plan.progress:
Techniques: string skipping with two and three notes per string up to 120, alternate picking to 124, legato trills with fingers 3-4 and 2-3 up to 104, finger pattern 1-4-2-3. Next: string skips inside scale positions, legato lines across strings.
Extended chords: Am7, Am9, D9, Gmaj7, Dm9 and G9 in sixteenth strumming up to 100, comping Am9-D9 and the turn to Gmaj7 over drums and bass. Next: 13th chords, shell voicings on a ii–V–I.
Scales: A Dorian in positions 1 to 3 joined on the G string, aiming for the 6th over D7; A Mixolydian aiming for the ♭7 over the G chord; the two compared in the same frets; D Dorian over Dm7-G7; notes named up to fret 15. Next: Phrygian and Lydian by the same method, positions 4 and 5.
CAGED: Am and D triads on all four string sets, A-G-D triads on three sets, triad notes as targets in a Dorian solo. Next: the inversions of one triad along one string set.

exercises.title: Skip a string, in stages
exercises.why: Skipping a string makes the pick travel twice as far between notes, so it trains the aim that wide phrases across a position need.

cells.text:
Press Play below to start the metronome. Pick down, up on each string, then jump over the next string, as the tab shows. Keep the strokes small, and let your wrist do the jump.
When the pick lands on the right string without you looking, try a faster stage. Use the Stage selector below to change the tempo, then press Play to start the metronome again.
If you hit the string in between, go back one stage.

exercises.title: Am7 and D9
exercises.why: A 9th chord is a 7th chord with one more note on top, so D9 goes wherever D7 goes and adds a colour above it.

cells.text: Press a chord box below to hear it, then fret each chord as shown. Change from Am7 to D9 and back until your fingers lift and land together.

Press Play below to start the metronome. After a bar of count-in, the lit box shows the chord: strum the pattern in the boxes, two bars of each chord. Your hand goes down and up four times a beat and misses the strings where the box shows a dot.
If a change comes late, keep your strumming hand going and catch the next beat 1.

tool.pattern: D . . U . U D U D . . U . U D U

exercises.title: A Dorian: find the 6th
exercises.why: A Dorian and A natural minor differ by one note, the 6th, so that note is the only place the mode can be heard: find it first, then aim for it.

cells.text:
Press Play below to start the backing: Am for eight bars, four in A natural minor, then four in A Dorian. Play each scale up and back down along with the neck, and listen for the bar where one note changes.
The faded note is the one to leave out: F♯ in the first half, F in the second.

cells.heading: Root on the low E string

cells.text: The note that changed is {{6}}: tap it on the neck below to hear it. This is the position with {{1}} on the low E string. Play it up and back down, then make up short phrases that pass through {{6}}.

Press Play below to start the drone on A. This is the same mode in the position with {{1}} on the A string: play it up and back down, and stop for a moment on each ringed {{6}}.
Keep going until your fingers reach for {{6}} without you looking for it.

exercises.title: Solo over Am7 and D7
exercises.why: F♯, the 6th of A Dorian, is the 3rd of D7, so landing on it as the chord changes makes one note say both the mode and the chord.

cells.text: Press Play below to start the backing, which switches between Am7 and D7. Improvise in A Dorian, in either position from the last exercise. Land on {{a}} when Am7 comes round and on {{f-sharp}} when D7 comes round.

Press Play below to start the band: drums, bass and keys on Am7 and D7. Play longer phrases now, and put the ringed {{6}} somewhere in each one: on the change, held, or passed through quickly.
If you lose the chords, stop on a ringed {{1}} and wait for Am7 to come round.

exercises.title: Name the notes, whole neck
exercises.why: A triad or a position starts from a note you can name, so naming notes anywhere on the neck is what lets you put either one in any key.

cells.text: Press Start in the game below. The game names a note: find it on the neck and play it, saying its name out loud. Keep going until the high frets come as quickly as the low ones.

exercises.title: Hammer and pull, fingers 3 and 4
exercises.why: Fingers 3 and 4 are the pair that moves apart least freely, so a trill on those two alone is the quickest way to make each one land by itself.

cells.text:
Press Play below to start the metronome and follow the tab. Pick once, then hammer finger 4 on and pull it off to finger 3, one note per beat, with no more picking. Rest your hand when it gets tired, then go again.
When the pulled-off note is as loud as the hammered one, try a faster stage. Use the Stage selector below to change the tempo, then press Play to start the metronome again.
If a note goes missing at a new stage, go back one stage.

exercises.title: Am and D on four string sets
exercises.why: A triad is three notes on three neighbouring strings, so every set of three strings holds the same chord in a new shape and a new register.

cells.text: Press Play below to start the backing and follow the tab: the Am triad on the top three strings, struck once per beat for a bar, then D for a bar. Keep going until the change from Am to D takes no thought.
Press Play below to start the backing: the same two chords one set of strings lower. The shapes are new, so let the tab lead for the first few rounds.
Press Play below to start the backing: the same chords on the A, D and G strings. Say the name of each chord as you strike it.

Press Play below to start the backing: the low three strings.
Then stop the backing and play Am on all four sets in a row, low to high, and D on the way back down. Same chord, four places: now try it with a chord you choose.

exercises.title: Triad notes in a Dorian solo
exercises.why: The notes of Am and D are all inside A Dorian, so the triads you just played are the places a solo over those two chords can land.

cells.text: Press Play below to start the backing, which switches between Am7 and D7. Improvise in A Dorian and end each phrase on a ringed note: a note of the Am triad over Am7, a note of the D triad over D7.

Press Play below to start the backing again. Now the ringed note is the 3rd of each chord: {{c}} over Am7 and {{f-sharp}} over D7. Aim every phrase at it.
The 3rd of D7 is the Dorian note from day 1, so this is the same aim with a second target.

Press Play below to start the band on Am7 and D7. Open a phrase with one of today's triads, carry on with the scale, and end on a note of the chord playing.
If a phrase ends on a note that sounds unfinished, move it one step up or down the scale.

exercises.title: Down-up picking, in stages
exercises.why: Picking down then up plays two notes with one swing of the hand, so the hand gets faster by making the swing smaller, not by working harder.

cells.text:
Press Play below to start the metronome. Pick each string down, up, down, up, and follow the arrows under the tab.
When your hand swings evenly with no stop between strings, try a faster stage. Use the Stage selector below to change the tempo, then press Play to start the metronome again.
If the up strokes get quieter than the down strokes, go back one stage.

exercises.title: Am9, D9, Gmaj7
exercises.why: A Dorian and G major are the same seven notes, so the two chords of the Dorian vamp are also the ii and the V of G: one more chord takes them home.

cells.text: Press a chord box below to hear it, then fret each chord as shown. Change from Am9 to D9 first, then from D9 to Gmaj7, until each pair moves without a stop in between.
Press Play below to start the metronome. Strum the pattern in the boxes: a bar of Am9, a bar of D9, then two bars of Gmaj7. Listen for the bar where the chords stop wanting to move on.

tool.pattern: D . D U . U D U

exercises.title: Join the Dorian positions
exercises.why: Each position starts on the notes where the one below ends, so one slide along one string carries a line from one position into the next.

cells.text: The neck below shows only the crossing from position 1 to position 2 of A Dorian. Climb position 1 from the low {{1}}. On the G string, slide up into position 2 and finish the climb there. Come back down the same way.
The same crossing one position higher: climb position 2, slide up the G string and finish in position 3. Then play both crossings in a row, from the low {{1}} in position 1 to the top of position 3.

Play the crossing from position 1 to 2 in other keys. Use the Key selector below to change the key.
When you change the key, the notes change but the crossing is the same slide on the G string. Stay in each key until the slide lands without you looking for it.

exercises.title: Climb through three positions
exercises.why: The 6th is in every position, so a solo can move up the neck and still land on it each time D7 comes round.

cells.text: Press Play below to start the backing. Start in position 1 and move up a position every few bars, crossing on the G string, until you are in position 3. Land on {{f-sharp}} when D7 comes round, wherever you are.
Press Play below to start the band on Am7 and D7. Start in position 3 and come down a position every few bars. End your last phrase on the lowest ringed {{1}}.

exercises.title: Fingers 1, 4, 2, 3
exercises.why: A pattern that sends finger 4 straight after finger 1 makes the hand open and close on every string, which is the move wide scale positions ask for.

cells.text:
Press Play below to start the metronome and follow the tab: frets 5, 8, 6 and 7 with fingers 1, 4, 2 and 3, on every string and back. The row under the tab shows the pick stroke for each note.
When the order needs no thought, try a faster stage. Use the Stage selector below to change the tempo, then press Play to start the metronome again.
If a finger lands late at a new stage, go back one stage and stay there a little longer.

exercises.title: A, G and D triads
exercises.why: A, G and D are the I, ♭VII and IV chords of A Mixolydian, and between them the three triads hold all seven notes of the mode.

cells.text: Press Play below to start the backing and follow the tab: each triad on the top three strings, struck once per beat for a bar. The chords go A, G, D and back to A.
Press Play below to start the backing: the same chords one set of strings lower. Keep going until you can look away from the tab for a whole round.

exercises.title: A Mixolydian: find the ♭7
exercises.why: Mixolydian is the major scale with one note lowered, the 7th, so day 1's method works again: find the one note that differs, then aim for it.

cells.text:
Press Play below to start the backing: A for eight bars, four in A major, then four in A Mixolydian. Play each scale up and back down along with the neck, and listen for the bar where one note changes.
The faded note is the one to leave out: G in the first half, G♯ in the second.

cells.heading: Root on the low E string

cells.text: The note that changed is {{b7}}: tap it on the neck below to hear it. This is the position with {{1}} on the low E string. Play it up and back down, then make up short phrases that stop on {{b7}} and step up to {{1}}.

Press Play below to start the drone on A. This is the same mode in the position with {{1}} on the A string. Hold each ringed {{b7}} against the drone, then let it step up to {{1}}.
Keep going until you can find {{b7}} from any {{1}} without looking.

exercises.title: Mixolydian over A, G and D
exercises.why: G, the ♭7 of A Mixolydian, is the root of the G chord, so landing on it as G comes round puts the mode's one changed note where it sounds most at home.

cells.text:
Press Play below to start the backing: A, G, D and A, two bars each. Improvise in A Mixolydian and land on the ringed note as each chord arrives.
The one to listen for is {{g}} over the G chord: it is the note you found in the last exercise.

Press Play below to start the band: A, G, D and A with drums, bass and keys. Play phrases that end on a ringed note, and try one that holds {{b7}} right through the G bar.
If you lose your place, stop on a ringed {{1}} and wait for the first bar to come round.

exercises.title: Hammer and pull, fingers 2 and 3
exercises.why: A pulled-off note is sounded by the finger leaving the string, so a trill is only even when the pull is as firm as the hammer.

cells.text:
Press Play below to start the metronome and follow the tab. Pick once, then hammer finger 3 on and pull it off to finger 2, one note per beat, with no more picking.
When both notes sound equally loud, try a faster stage. Use the Stage selector below to change the tempo, then press Play to start the metronome again.
If the pulled-off note gets quiet at a new stage, go back one stage and stay there a little longer.

exercises.title: Comp the Dorian vamp
exercises.why: Comping is leaving room: with only drums and bass under you every strum you leave out can be heard, so the gaps become part of the rhythm.

cells.text:
Press Play below to start the metronome. Strum the pattern in the boxes, two bars of Am9 and two of D9.
When the change no longer makes your strumming hand wait, try a faster stage. Use the Stage selector below to change the tempo, then press Play to start the metronome again.
If a change comes late, keep the hand going and catch the next beat 1.

tool.pattern: D . . U . U D U D . . U . U D U

cells.text: Press Play below to start the band: drums and bass, and the chord boxes light as the bars go by. You are the only one playing the chords. Leave some strums out, and keep your hand moving through the gaps.

exercises.title: Dorian or Mixolydian: the 3rd
exercises.why: A Dorian and A Mixolydian share six notes and differ only in the 3rd, so moving that one note a fret turns the minor mode into the major one.

cells.text:
Press Play below to start the backing: a drone on A for eight bars, four in A Dorian, then four in A Mixolydian. Play each scale up and back down along with the neck, and listen for the bar where the 3rd moves.
The faded note is the one to leave out: C♯ in the first half, C in the second.
This is A Dorian in the position with {{1}} on the low E string, with {{b3}} ringed. Play the position up and back down, then make up a few phrases that end on {{b3}}.

The same frets in A Mixolydian: the 3rd has moved up a fret, to {{3}}. Play the phrases you just made up again and end them on the new 3rd.
Then slide into it from one fret below. {{c}} is not in A Mixolydian: it is the minor 3rd you just left, and blues players slide from it up to {{3}} all the time.

exercises.title: Two bands, two modes
exercises.why: A band's chords choose the mode for you: Am7 holds C and the A chord holds C♯, so the same position needs its 3rd moved when the band changes.

cells.text: Press Play below to start the band on Am7 and D7. Improvise in A Dorian and lean on the two ringed notes, {{b3}} and {{6}}: the 3rd makes it minor and the 6th makes it Dorian.

Press Play below to start the band on A, G and D. Stay in the same frets and improvise in A Mixolydian, leaning on {{3}} and {{b7}}.
When you change the band, the root stays on A and one note under your fingers moves a fret: the 3rd.

exercises.title: Skip a string, three notes
exercises.why: With three notes on a string the pick leaves on a down stroke one time and on an up stroke the next, so both ways of crossing to a new string get trained.

cells.text:
Press Play below to start the metronome. Pick three notes on each string and keep the strokes going down, up, down, up across the jump, as the arrows under the tab show.
When the jump feels the same after a down stroke as after an up stroke, try a faster stage. Use the Stage selector below to change the tempo, then press Play to start the metronome again.
If you hit the string in between, go back one stage.

exercises.title: Dm9 and G9
exercises.why: Dm9 and G9 are Dm7 and G7 with a 9th added, so they fit the same vamp and only the top of each chord changes colour.

cells.text: Press a chord box below to hear it, then fret each chord as shown. Change from Dm9 to G9 and back until your fingers lift and land together.
Press Play below to start the metronome. Strum the pattern in the boxes, two bars of each chord. Stay on it until the change stops interrupting your strumming hand.

tool.pattern: D . . U . U D U D . . U . U D U

exercises.title: D Dorian on the neck
exercises.why: A mode is a shape counted from its root, so moving the root from A to D moves every position with it, and the 6th keeps its place inside each one.

cells.text: The whole neck is drawn above the position: the framed part is position 1 of D Dorian. Play it up and back down from the low {{1}}, and notice it is the shape you know from A, further up the neck. The ringed {{6}} is where your fingers expect it.

The neck below shows only the crossing from position 1 to position 2 of D Dorian. Climb position 1, slide up the G string as you did in A, and finish the climb in position 2. Come back down the same way.

Press Play below to start the drone. Play the position on the neck up and back down, and end on a ringed {{1}}.
Then try the other variant. Use the Variant selector below to change it, then press Play to start the drone again, now on the new root.
When you change the variant, your hand stays in the same frets: this is position 3 of A Dorian, one note has moved a fret, and the ringed notes are in new places.

exercises.title: Solo over Dm7 and G7
exercises.why: B, the 6th of D Dorian, is the 3rd of G7: the job F♯ did over D7, so the aim you built in A works here with new note names.

cells.text: Press Play below to start the backing, which switches between Dm7 and G7. Improvise in D Dorian. Land on {{d}} when Dm7 comes round and on {{b}} when G7 comes round.

Press Play below to start the band on Dm7 and G7. Play a phrase you liked in A this week, moved to D, then carry on from it.
When you change the key, the notes are new but the ringed {{6}} still lands on the second chord.

exercises.title: Skip a string, day 1 again
exercises.why: The same drill starting a stage above day 1 is the plainest way to feel what a week of string skipping has done.

cells.text:
Press Play below to start the metronome: day 1's drill, starting a stage higher than day 1 did. Pick down, up on each string, then jump over the next string.
When the pick lands on the right string without you looking, try a faster stage. Use the Stage selector below to change the tempo, then press Play to start the metronome again.
Notice how much less you watch your picking hand than you did on day 1.

exercises.title: Comp for the jam
exercises.why: The same two chords sound like a Dorian vamp while they loop and like a ii–V the moment Gmaj7 follows them, so the last two bars change what the first six meant.

cells.text: Press Play below to start the metronome. Strum the pattern in the boxes: Am9 and D9 three times round, a bar each, then two bars of Gmaj7.

tool.pattern: D . D U . U D U

cells.text: Press Play below to start the band: drums and bass, and the chord boxes light as the bars go by. You are the only one playing the chords. Leave strums out in the vamp, then play every strum when Gmaj7 arrives.

exercises.title: Triads with your eyes off the tab
exercises.why: Looking away makes your hand find each shape from the one before it, not from the screen, which is how a triad gets found in the middle of a song.

cells.text: Press Play below to start the backing: day 4's triads on the top three strings. Play with your eyes off the tab, and check it only when a shape will not come.
Press Play below to start the backing: the same chords on the A, D and G strings, a set day 4 left out. Find each shape before its bar starts, and say the chord's name as you strike it.

exercises.title: The jam
exercises.why: Each day gave you one thing to aim a phrase at (the 6th, a triad note, the ♭7, a crossing), so a solo is choosing which one each phrase goes for.

cells.text: Press Play below to start the backing: day 1's Am7 and D7. Land on {{f-sharp}} when D7 comes round, in any position you like. Notice how much sooner your fingers find it than they did on day 1.
Press Play below to start the band on A, G and D. Improvise in A Mixolydian and hold the ringed {{b7}} through the G bar.

Press Play below to start the band, back on Am7 and D7. Play one long solo in A Dorian that climbs from position 1 to position 3 and comes back down. Choose what each phrase aims for: the 6th, a triad note or a crossing. Keep the one phrase you like best for next week.
